newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany faces tax limbo until 1998 election.
newsitem.headline: Germany faces tax limbo until 1998 election.

text.p: Germany's tax reform of the century is dead: Long live the tax reform.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel refuses to give up on his plan to cut 30 billion marks in taxes even though the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have condemned it to political limbo by blocking it in parliament's conflict resolution process.
"We'll keep the big tax reform on the agenda," Waigel said on Thursday, insisting the government still wanted to bring in as much of the reform as possible.
"If this doesn't happen, then the SPD alone must bear the responsibility." he said. "The SPD is moving at a snail's pace when it comes to tax reform."

But Waigel knows full well he stands no chance of passing his tax cuts into law before the general election in September 1998 -- even if he forces parliament's mediation committee to reconvene this autumn.

Given today's power relations -- Chancellor Helmut Kohl has a slim majority in the lower house and the SPD governs in a majority of federal states represented in the Bundesrat upper house -- consensus is needed to pass fundamental tax reforms.
The SPD, confident it can secure control of both houses of parliament next year to assume unchecked power, sees no reason to make life easy for Kohl's tiring government.

SPD tax negotiators Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier and Peter Struck said the government's tax proposals were "deeply unjust and financially irresponsible". They plan to launch their own tax reform after their hoped-for victory next year.

The prospect of over a year of stalemate in which the Kohl coalition will be hamstrung on tax reforms has raised howls of protest from businesses, labour leaders and economists calling for urgent action to end Germany's economic malaise.

The Federation of Germany Industry (BDI) slammed the situation as a "tax policy fiasco" which would mean bankruptcy for many businesses -- especially the Mittelstand of small- and medium-sized companies.
"The Mittelstand, the unemployed, and those who are about to lose their jobs, should sue those who have acted out of party political interests," the BDI said in a statement.
Germany's current tax system is seen as the worst of all worlds -- driving jobs abroad, distorting investment incentives and offering huge tax loopholes for the rich.

Economists say the government tax reform would have boosted German economic growth by as much as half a percentage point a year in the long run. Meanwhile, uncertainty over its fate has crippled job-creating investment.

For now there looks to be no end to Germany's problem of "jobless growth" in which the economy expands, but suffocatingly high labour costs mean no inroads can be made into record post-war unemployment of over four million.

German newspaper commentators on Thursday played up the contrast between the can-do pragmatism of U.S. politicians -- who face a similar division of power between the two houses of Congress but have still agreed on $95 billion in tax cuts.
"There could barely be more contrasting reports on the ability of countries to implement reform," the Handelsblatt business daily said.

"While the U.S. government and congress are agreeing massive tax cuts...linked in to a budget compromise, Bonn politicians have simultaneously allowed the tax reform which was correctly dubbed by all experts as the reform of the century to collapse quietly," the newspaper added.
There have been isolated calls -- from BDI head Hans-Olaf Henkel and former Economics Minister Otto Graf Lambsdorff -- for reforms to streamline Germany's political system.
But those calls have been rejected by mainstream politicians, who think they would have too much to lose by changing the current system.
Instead they hailed a separate deal reached after 15 hours of talks in the mediation committee to abolish a capital trading tax on companies.
But even here, the dispute had already dragged on for over two years. And it took a prod from the constitutional court to forge an agreement.

What did it take so long to agree on? Apparently, much of the time was spent arguing over whether a constitutional amendment linked to the tax's abolition should contain the word "appropriate" or "comparable".
